title: Neurodivergence — Reading the Map Without the Legend
hook: An autistic colleague who never meets your eye may be listening harder than anyone in the room; your map of faces was drawn for a different country.
why:
Almost everything in this book so far has assumed a common body language: that people look at you when they listen, that a flat face means a flat mood, that stillness means attention and fidgeting means boredom. For most people, most of the time, those assumptions are close enough to be useful. For a sizeable minority they are simply wrong.

Neurodivergence is the umbrella term for brains that work differently from the majority, including autism, ADHD, dyslexia and related conditions. The World Health Organization estimates that about one child in a hundred is autistic, and many adults, particularly older men, were never diagnosed. ADHD is more common still. You almost certainly work with, live near or love someone whose body speaks a different dialect.

This chapter does not teach you to spot neurodivergence, which would be both unreliable and intrusive. It teaches you to notice when your readings are built on a map that does not fit, why first impressions of autistic people go wrong, why misunderstanding runs in both directions, how to re-read eye contact, movement and expression, and what to do instead of guessing.

teach.h: A different dialect, not a broken one.
teach.p:
Every reading in this book rests on a baseline, as Part I insisted: you learn what is normal for a person before you interpret a change. The trouble with neurodivergent people is not that they have no baseline. It is that their baseline differs from the one you carry around without noticing, the one built from thousands of interactions with people whose bodies behave much like yours.

An autistic man may look away while listening, speak in a level tone about something he cares about intensely, and stand very still or move in ways that soothe him. A man with ADHD may jiggle his leg, doodle or pace while thinking hard. Neither is sending the message a neurotypical reader would assume. The behaviour is the same; the meaning is not.

It helps to think of these as dialects. A dialect is not a broken version of a language. It is a complete system with its own rules, and speakers of different dialects misunderstand each other in predictable ways. Many autistic people now describe themselves this way, and the research reviewed in this chapter supports the idea that the problem lies between people rather than inside one of them.

Language matters here too. Many autistic people prefer to be called autistic rather than a person with autism, seeing it as part of who they are; others prefer the opposite. The safe course is to follow the person's own words. The figure here looks aside while someone speaks. In one person this is distraction. In another it is the way he listens best.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if neurodivergent people's behaviour carried the same meanings as everyone else's. The studies in this chapter show systematic differences in eye contact, movement and expression that do not mean what a neurotypical reader assumes.

teach.h: First impressions go wrong in seconds.
teach.p:
In 2017 Noah Sasson and his colleagues filmed autistic and non-autistic adults taking part in a mock audition and showed short clips, a few seconds long, to hundreds of observers. The observers rated the autistic adults less favourably on several counts. They were seen as more awkward and less likeable, and observers said they would be less willing to talk to them, live near them or sit next to them.

The most revealing part of the study was what happened when observers saw only a transcript of what each person said. The difference disappeared, and on some measures the autistic participants were rated more favourably. Their words were as good as anyone's. The negative impression came from how they looked and sounded while saying them: their gaze, their expressions, their movement and the music of their voices.

These judgments were made in seconds, without any information about diagnosis. The observers were not prejudiced against autism as such. They were doing what this book has described from the start, forming impressions from thin slices of behaviour, and applying a map that did not fit.

The practical lesson is that your first impression of someone who seems awkward, cold or odd is especially likely to be wrong if that person is neurodivergent. Before you decide, look at what they actually say and do. The figure here stands at rest, neither warm nor cold. A reader who sees coldness here is supplying it.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if impressions of autistic adults were as negative from transcripts as from video. Sasson and colleagues found the negative impressions came from the clips, not from what the people said.

teach.p:
For decades, autism was described as a deficit in social understanding: autistic people were said to lack the ability to read other minds. In 2012 the autistic sociologist Damian Milton challenged this framing. He argued that when an autistic and a non-autistic person misunderstand each other, the failure runs both ways. The non-autistic person struggles to read the autistic person just as much, but only one of them is labelled as having a problem. He called this the double empathy problem.

In 2020 Catherine Crompton and her colleagues tested the idea. They asked people to pass a story along a chain, each person retelling it to the next, as in the children's game of telephone. Chains made up entirely of autistic people passed on the information about as accurately as chains made up entirely of non-autistic people. Mixed chains, alternating between the two, lost the most detail. Participants also reported less rapport in mixed pairs.

In other words, autistic people communicated effectively with each other. The breakdown happened at the boundary between dialects, not inside one of them. A later replication by the same group found the same pattern.

This changes the reader's job. If you find someone hard to read, that is information about the meeting of your two styles, not a verdict on them. It also means the effort of bridging the gap should be shared, not left to the person who is in the minority. The figures here stand at an angle, each reading the other. Both may be getting it wrong.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people communicated poorly with each other as well as with non-autistic people. Crompton and colleagues found autistic chains as accurate as non-autistic ones, with the losses concentrated in mixed chains.
teach.pullQuote: If you find someone hard to read, that is information about the meeting of your two styles, not a verdict on them.

teach.p:
No signal in this book is more often misread in neurodivergent people than eye contact. The chapter on gaze in Part I described research in which autistic adults reported that eye contact felt intense, uncomfortable or distracting, and that they looked away in order to concentrate on what was being said. Many describe sustained eye contact as overwhelming, like trying to listen to someone while a bright light shines in your face.

The usual readings of averted gaze are evasion, boredom, shyness or deceit. The chapter on deception in Part I explained why gaze aversion is a poor sign of lying in anyone. In autistic people it is often the opposite of disengagement: they are giving the conversation their full attention by removing a source of distraction.

Some autistic people have learned to fake eye contact, looking at the bridge of the nose or the mouth, or forcing themselves to hold a gaze while counting seconds. This can make them seem more conventional, but it costs effort and attention, and it often leaves them with less capacity for the conversation itself. The next chapter, on masking, looks at that cost.

For a reader, the change is simple. Stop treating eye contact as evidence of attention, honesty or respect, at least until you know the person. If you need to know whether someone has understood, ask, or look at what they do afterwards. Never insist that someone look at you. The figure here looks down and away. In a conversation with an autistic colleague, this may be the posture of someone who is following every word.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people who looked away were generally less attentive or less honest. Their own accounts, and research on gaze and concentration, suggest that looking away often helps them attend.

teach.p:
Neurotypical readers tend to read stillness as attention and movement as restlessness or boredom. For many neurodivergent people the relationship runs the other way.

Part II's chapter on self-soothing described stimming: repetitive movements such as rocking, hand-flapping, finger-tapping or fiddling with an object, which many autistic people use to regulate their arousal and focus. Autistic adults describe these movements as calming, as a way of expressing emotion, and sometimes as a source of joy. Suppressing them, often because others stare, can make it harder to cope.

For ADHD, there is experimental evidence that movement supports thinking. In 2015 Dustin Sarver, Mark Rapport, Michael Kofler and their colleagues measured how much children moved while doing tasks that taxed working memory. Children with ADHD who moved more tended to perform better, while children without ADHD tended to perform worse when they moved more. The authors suggested that, for children with ADHD, movement may help keep the brain alert enough to work.

The implication is clear. A colleague who jiggles a leg, clicks a pen, doodles or paces while you talk may be listening better because of it. Asking them to sit still may cost them the very attention you wanted. The figure here sits with one heel raised, the beginning of a bounce. In one person it is nerves. In another it is how concentration feels from the inside.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if movement always reduced attention. Sarver and colleagues found that, for children with ADHD, more movement went with better working memory performance, though the study involved children rather than adults.

teach.h: Faces and voices that do not follow the script.
teach.p:
Neurodivergent people may also express emotion differently in their faces and voices. In 2016 Rebecca Brewer, Geoffrey Bird and their colleagues asked autistic and non-autistic people to pose facial expressions of emotion, then asked observers to identify them. The expressions posed by autistic people were recognised less accurately, and, strikingly, autistic observers found them just as hard to read as non-autistic observers did.

The researchers concluded that autistic people's expressions were not following a shared autistic style but were individual. Each person's face had its own way of showing feeling. That fits what many autistic people say about themselves: that their face does not always show what they feel, or shows it in a way others misread.

Voices vary too. An autistic man may speak in a level tone about something he loves, or sound blunt when he means to be clear. A man with ADHD may interrupt because he fears losing a thought, not because he does not respect yours. Literal speech, missed hints and unusual timing are common.

The safest approach is to take words at face value and to read changes against the person's own baseline, not against a general template. A flat face is not a sign of a flat mood until you know that, in this person, it is. The figure here tilts his head slightly while listening. On one face this would read as interest. On another it might be the only sign of interest you will see.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if autistic people's facial expressions were as readable as anyone's. Brewer and colleagues found their posed expressions were recognised less accurately by autistic and non-autistic observers alike.

teach.p:
If your map does not fit, the answer is not a better map of autistic or ADHD body language. It is to stop relying on maps and start asking.

Ask rather than infer. If you are unsure whether someone is interested, upset or finished, ask plainly: Do you want to keep going with this, or stop here? Most neurodivergent people find direct questions a relief. State your own meaning rather than hinting. If something is urgent, say so; if you are joking, say so; if you are disappointed, say what about. Hints and tone that most people decode automatically may be missed.

Adjust the setting. Many people find it easier to talk side by side than face to face, as Part III described, or to talk while walking, or to follow up in writing. Offer an agenda before a meeting. Give time to think before an answer is needed. Avoid unexpected touch. Do not demand eye contact.

Above all, do not diagnose. Noticing that someone's style is unusual is useful; deciding that they are autistic, and treating them accordingly, is not your call and is often wrong. The aim is to read every person as an individual and to make it easier for people of every kind to be understood. The figures here stand side by side, looking the same way, the arrangement that makes many conversations easier for everyone.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if asking directly and stating meaning plainly made conversations with neurodivergent people no easier. Autistic people's own accounts, and the double empathy research, suggest that clarity and shared effort reduce misunderstanding.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, no gaze required
poseGallery.dontCaption: Insisting he look you in the eye
poseGallery.annotation: Eye contact is not evidence of attention. Arrangements that take gaze out of the conversation help many people listen better.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Deciding a flat face means he is not interested
poseGallery.annotation: A flat face is not a flat mood until you know this person. Ask, and take the answer at face value.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Telling a colleague to sit still
poseGallery.annotation: For some people, movement is how attention works. Asking them to stop may cost the focus you wanted.

poseGallery.doCaption: Alongside, talking while looking at the task
poseGallery.dontCaption: Crouching close and demanding eye contact
poseGallery.annotation: Many autistic children listen best without a face pushed close to theirs. Sit beside, look at the work together and let the gaze go.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, looking at something shared
poseGallery.annotation: A shared object to look at takes the pressure off eye contact. Many conversations go further side by side.

caseStudy:
Liam, thirty-four, manages a small software team. When Ravi joined, Liam formed an impression within a week. Ravi rarely looked at anyone in meetings, answered questions in a few flat words, never laughed at the team's jokes and sometimes said things like That approach will not work, without softening it. Liam decided he was disengaged, possibly arrogant, and began to wonder whether the hire had been a mistake.

Then he read Ravi's first written design review. It was the most careful document anyone on the team had produced, and it caught two problems Liam had missed. He asked Ravi for a one-to-one, and, rather than giving feedback about his manner, asked how he preferred to work.

Ravi told him, a little warily, that he was autistic. He said he looked away in meetings because faces distracted him from what people were saying, that he found the jokes hard to follow when several people talked at once, and that he said things directly because he assumed people wanted to know. He asked whether he could get agendas in advance and give some of his input in writing.

Liam agreed. He started sending agendas the day before, asking for written comments, and saying plainly what he meant instead of hinting. He stopped reading Ravi's gaze as a verdict. Within a few months, Ravi was the person the team relied on for reviews, and Liam had noticed that two other team members liked the agendas just as much. He also noticed how quickly he had been ready to write someone off on the strength of a manner.
observe: Notice someone this week whose manner you find hard to read, and write down what they actually said, separately from how they said it.
Notice your own reading of eye contact: whether you take looking away as a sign of boredom, shyness or evasion.
Notice people who move while they think, such as pacing, doodling or tapping, and whether their contributions suffer for it.
Notice how often you hint rather than say what you mean, and whether anyone misses the hint.

drills.name: Words Without the Body
steps: Think of a colleague or acquaintance whose manner you find awkward or cold.
Write down three things they said recently, word for word if you can.
Read the words back as if from a stranger, without picturing their face or voice.
Note whether your impression of them changes.
Decide on one thing you will judge by their words and actions rather than their manner.
variations: Do the drill with a colleague whose manner you like, too, and notice whether their words alone are as strong as you thought.
Read a transcript or the written minutes of a meeting before you watch or remember it, and compare your impression of each speaker.
Ask a trusted friend to read the words you wrote down, without knowing who said them, and tell you their impression.

drills.name: Say It Plainly
steps: For one day, notice each time you hint instead of stating what you want or mean.
Rewrite three of those hints as plain statements.
Use one of the plain versions in a real conversation.
Note how the other person responded.
variations: Ask a colleague whether they would prefer you to be more direct with them, and use their answer.
Rewrite one email you are about to send so that the request is in the first sentence, and notice whether the reply comes faster.
Notice one hint someone gives you this week that you could easily have missed, and how you would have preferred to be told.

drills.name: Offer the Format
steps: Before your next meeting or important conversation, send a short agenda or the key question in writing.
Offer a choice of how to respond: in the meeting, by message afterwards, or in a walk-and-talk.
Notice who takes up which option.
Ask one person afterwards whether it helped.
variations: Offer people the choice of a walking meeting or a seated one for your next one-to-one, and notice who chooses which.
Send questions for a discussion in advance, and invite written answers from anyone who prefers them.
After a meeting, send a short written summary of what was agreed, so that people who process better in writing have it.

drills.name: Gaze Audit
steps: In your next three conversations, notice how much eye contact you expect and how you react when it is missing.
Each time someone looks away, ask yourself what else might explain it.
Write down one occasion when you assumed something about gaze that turned out to be wrong.
Keep the note where you will see it.
variations: In one conversation this week, deliberately look at something shared, such as a screen or a view, rather than the other person's face, and notice how it feels.
Notice a child or young person looking away while you talk to them, and resist asking them to look at you.
Ask someone you know well how they feel about eye contact, and listen to the answer.

quiz.q: A manager says that a team member who never meets his eye in meetings is probably not paying attention. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is right, because eye contact is the most reliable sign of attention in any person
For many autistic people, looking away is how they concentrate on what is being said
Averted gaze is a reliable sign of deceit, so the team member is likely hiding something
Gaze means nothing in anyone, so managers should never pay any attention to it at all
quiz.explain: Many autistic adults report that eye contact is intense or distracting and that they look away in order to listen. Gaze is a poor guide to attention or honesty until you know the person's baseline.

quiz.q: What did Sasson and colleagues find when observers judged autistic adults from transcripts alone?
options: The autistic adults were rated even more harshly than they had been from the video clips
The negative impressions disappeared, and on some measures autistic adults were rated more favourably
Observers could tell from the transcripts alone which speakers were autistic and which were not
Transcripts produced the same ratings as video, so the impressions came from the words
quiz.explain: The negative first impressions came from how the autistic adults looked and sounded in short clips, not from what they said. Their words were as well received as anyone's.

quiz.q: In Crompton and colleagues' study, which chains passed on a story least accurately?
options: Chains made up entirely of autistic people
Chains made up entirely of non-autistic people
Mixed chains, alternating autistic and non-autistic people
All the chains lost information at exactly the same rate
quiz.explain: Autistic chains were about as accurate as non-autistic ones. The losses were greatest in mixed chains, which fits Milton's idea that misunderstanding happens between dialects rather than inside one.

quiz.q: What does Milton's double empathy problem propose?
options: Autistic people have twice as much empathy as others, which overwhelms them
Non-autistic people should learn to imitate autistic body language exactly
Empathy can be measured twice, once from the face and once from the voice
Misunderstanding between autistic and non-autistic people runs in both directions
quiz.explain: Milton argued that difficulties in communication arise between people with different ways of being, not from a deficit in one of them. Both sides struggle to read the other.

quiz.q: During a planning meeting, a colleague bounces his leg, doodles constantly and rarely looks up, yet his comments are sharp and relevant. What fits this chapter best?
options: Ask him privately to sit still and look at the speaker, so he seems more engaged in meetings
Let him be, since for some people movement and looking away help them concentrate
Conclude that he is bored, and give his part of the project to someone more attentive
Raise his behaviour with the rest of the team, so that everyone can help him to change
quiz.explain: His contributions show he is attending. For some people, especially with ADHD or autism, movement and averted gaze support concentration, and suppressing them can cost the attention you want.

quiz.q: A new team member who has told you he is autistic gives short, blunt answers and seems uncomfortable in group discussion. What is the most useful step?
options: Ask how he prefers to communicate, and offer agendas and written options
Coach him to smile more and soften his answers, so others warm to him
Avoid involving him in discussions, so that he is not made uncomfortable
Explain to the team that he cannot read people, so that they make allowances
quiz.explain: Asking about preferences and offering formats that suit him shares the work of bridging the gap. Coaching him to perform a different style places the whole burden on him.

quiz.q: What did Brewer, Bird and colleagues find when observers tried to identify facial expressions posed by autistic people?
options: Autistic observers read them easily, while non-autistic observers could not read them at all
They were hard for everyone to read, which suggested each person's face had its own style
They were read more accurately than expressions posed by non-autistic people in the study
They could not be read because the autistic participants declined to pose any expressions
quiz.explain: Autistic people's posed expressions were recognised less accurately by autistic and non-autistic observers alike. The researchers concluded that the expressions were individual rather than following a shared autistic style.

quiz.q: A supply teacher tells an autistic nine-year-old to look at him while he explains a task, and the boy becomes distressed. What fits this chapter best?
options: Insist more firmly, since children need to learn to make eye contact with teachers
Stop asking for eye contact, and judge his listening by what he does with the task
Send him out of the room, since distress during instructions is a form of defiance
Crouch closer to his desk, so that it is easier for him to look at the teacher's face
quiz.explain: Many autistic people look away in order to listen, and demanding eye contact can raise distress. What a child does with the instructions shows whether he heard them far better than where his eyes were.

quiz.q: A parent says that a child who keeps moving while doing homework cannot be concentrating properly. What did Sarver and colleagues find?
options: Children with ADHD who moved more during demanding memory tasks tended to perform better
All children performed worse whenever they moved, so stillness always helps concentration
Movement made no difference at all to the performance of any child who took part in the study
Only children without ADHD benefited from moving, while children with ADHD did much worse
quiz.explain: Children with ADHD who moved more while doing working-memory tasks tended to perform better, which suggests that movement can support thinking for some people rather than competing with it. It does not mean that every movement helps every child.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific person whose manner you have found hard to read or have judged quickly: a colleague, a relative, someone at a club. Describe what you noticed about their eye contact, expression, voice or movement, and what you concluded. Now write down what they actually said and did, separate from how they came across. Could your reading have been built on a map that does not fit them? What one thing could you ask them, or change, to understand them better?
reflection.guidance: You do not need to know or guess whether the person is neurodivergent. The point is to notice where your impression rests on manner rather than substance, and to find a way to ask instead of infer. Be specific about the moment and about what you could do differently next time.

failureMode: The first failure is to read averted gaze as evasion, boredom or disrespect, when for many people it is how they listen. The second is to trust a first impression of someone who seems awkward or cold, when research shows such impressions are built on manner rather than substance. The third is to treat misunderstanding as the other person's deficit, when it runs in both directions. The fourth is to ask someone to sit still, look up or smile more, when their movement or stillness may be what lets them think. The fifth is to hint and expect to be understood. And the sixth is to diagnose: deciding someone is autistic or has ADHD, and treating them as a category rather than a person.

moreCases.title: The student who paced
moreCases.scene:
Kieran, nineteen, is in his first year of an engineering degree. He was diagnosed with ADHD at fourteen, and he has told the university's
  disability service, which has sent a short note to his department. In the weekly lab briefing, forty students stand around benches while a
  demonstrator, Dr Hale, explains the experiment. Kieran stands at the back. After a few minutes he begins to move: shifting his weight, walking a few
  steps along the wall and back, turning a pen over in his fingers. He is listening hard. It is how he listens.

  In the third week, Dr Hale stops mid-sentence and says, in front of everyone, "If you can't stand still, perhaps you could wait outside." Several
  students laugh. Kieran goes red, stands rigidly still for the rest of the briefing, and finds afterwards that he cannot remember the second half of
  the instructions. His experiment goes wrong. He gets the lowest mark in the group.

  The next week he stands at the back again, holding himself still with his arms folded and his jaw tight. He misses half the briefing again.
  He stops asking questions in labs, and starts to wonder whether he is cut out for the course.

  His personal tutor, Dr Mensah, notices his marks dropping and asks to see him. Kieran tells her what happened. She asks whether Dr Hale had seen the
  note from the disability service. Kieran does not know.

Kieran's school had let him stand at the back of the class for years. Nobody at the university had told him that this might be a problem, and he had not thought to mention it.

He had also been told by a friend in the second year that Dr Hale was strict but fair, and he spends the evening trying to work out what he had done that was unfair to Dr Hale.

In the second lab, a classmate whispers that he should just take something to calm down. Kieran does not reply.
moreCases.misread:
Dr Hale read Kieran's pacing and fidgeting as inattention and disrespect, and corrected it in public. Kieran read the correction as proof that his way of listening was unacceptable, and tried to stop it, which made listening harder.

The students who laughed read the correction as a joke at the expense of a fidgety classmate. None of them knew that Kieran had been listening more carefully than most of them.

And Kieran read his own need to move as a weakness he should be able to overcome by effort, which is what he had been told, in one way or another, for most of his school life.

Dr Hale had also read the note from the disability service, it turned out, months earlier, and forgotten it. A note is not the same as a changed habit.
moreCases.betterRead:
Sarver and colleagues found that children with ADHD who moved more during working-memory tasks tended to perform better, which suggests that for some people movement supports thinking rather than competing with it. Kieran's pacing was the opposite of inattention. Holding himself still took so much effort that there was little left for the instructions. The better reading, which Dr Mensah helped bring about, began with the note that Dr Hale had not read. Dr Hale apologised to Kieran privately, and the department agreed that students could stand, move at the back of the room or hold something in their hands during briefings, and that written instructions would be posted before each lab. Several other students began using the back wall too. Kieran's marks recovered. Dr Hale said later that he had learned to stop reading stillness as attention in anyone.

Kieran also started telling new lecturers at the start of each module that he might move around, which took the surprise out of it.

The posted instructions turned out to help almost everyone, including two international students who had been struggling to follow the spoken briefings.

moreCases.title: The veterinary nurse who seemed cold
moreCases.scene:
Rosie, thirty-one, is a veterinary nurse at a busy practice, and she is autistic. She is meticulous, gentle with frightened animals and
  usually the last to leave, checking on the ones staying overnight. Her face tends to stay still, and her voice is level whatever she is saying. She
  explains things clearly and precisely, and she does not usually smile when she is concentrating.

  One afternoon she has to tell an elderly man, Mr Patel, that his dog's blood tests show kidney failure and that the vet would like to talk to him
  about the options. She explains the results carefully, in a calm, even voice, looking at the screen rather than at him. Mr Patel goes very quiet.
  Afterwards he tells the receptionist that the nurse "didn't seem to care at all", and writes a complaint saying she treated his dog like a set of
  numbers.

  The practice manager, Gill, reads the complaint and is inclined to agree that Rosie can come across as cold. She considers sending her on a course
  about client communication. Then she remembers that Rosie stayed until nine the previous Friday with a cat that was not expected to survive the night,
  talking to it quietly and stroking its head.

  Gill asks Rosie to come and talk about the complaint, and is careful to start by saying that she knows how much Rosie cares about the animals.

Rosie had in fact noticed that Mr Patel had gone quiet, and had wondered whether she should stop. She had decided that he needed the information, and carried on, because that was what she would have wanted.

She had also printed out the blood results for Mr Patel and highlighted the important numbers, so that he could read them again at home. He had left them on the counter.
moreCases.misread:
Mr Patel read Rosie's still face, level voice and gaze towards the screen as indifference to his dog and to him. Gill's first reading was that Rosie needed to learn to show warmth, which treated the difference as her deficit alone.

Rosie, for her part, had read Mr Patel's silence as him taking in the information, which was partly true, and had no way to read the hurt that went with it.

The receptionist who passed on the complaint read it as confirmation of something she had half thought herself, because Rosie rarely joined in the chat at the front desk.
moreCases.betterRead:
Brewer, Bird and colleagues found that autistic people's posed expressions were hard for everyone to read, autistic observers included, because each person's face had its own way of showing feeling. Rosie's care was real and visible in what she did, but her face and voice did not follow the script Mr Patel expected. The double empathy problem cuts both ways: he could not read her, and she had no way of knowing that he needed something her face was not giving. The better approach, which Gill and Rosie agreed together, did not ask Rosie to perform expressions she did not feel. Rosie chose to add a sentence to difficult conversations that put her care into words: "I know this is hard news. I've got very fond of Biscuit." Where she could, she sat beside clients rather than across the screen. Gill also rang Mr Patel to explain that Rosie had looked after his dog with great care. He came back the next week and asked for her by name.

Rosie said afterwards that having one sentence ready made difficult conversations easier for her too, because she no longer worried that clients were misreading her.

moreCases.title: The call that went perfectly
moreCases.scene:
Femi, thirty-eight, is an account manager at a company that builds data systems. He is sitting in on a video call between the company's lead
  engineer, Ines, and a client's technical lead, Martin. Both are autistic, and both have mentioned it in passing in earlier emails. The call is to
  agree the design of a complex data migration.

  To Femi, the call is excruciating. Neither Ines nor Martin makes small talk. Martin's camera is pointed slightly off to the side, and Ines looks at
  her second screen most of the time. They speak in short, precise sentences, with long silences while one of them thinks. Nobody smiles. When Ines
  says that Martin's proposed schedule is unrealistic, Martin says "Agreed," and they move on. Femi keeps trying to fill the silences with friendly
  remarks, which both of them ignore.

  After forty minutes, the call ends abruptly when they have finished the agenda. Femi is sure it has gone badly. He emails his manager to warn that the
  client relationship may be in trouble, and drafts an apology to Martin for the "tense" meeting.

  Before he sends it, an email arrives from Martin, copied to Ines. It says it was the most productive technical meeting he has had in a year, and
  attaches a list of agreed actions that is more complete than Femi's notes.

Femi had also been asked by his manager to "keep the relationship warm", and had understood that to mean filling the call with friendly chat.

At one point, Ines types a question into the chat instead of saying it aloud, and Martin answers in the chat too. Femi reads it as the two of them avoiding talking to each other.
moreCases.misread:
Femi read the absence of small talk, smiles and eye contact, and the long silences, as tension and a relationship going wrong. He read his own attempts to fill the silences as helpful, when they were interruptions to two people thinking.

His manager, reading Femi's warning email, nearly arranged a call with the client's director to smooth things over, which would have confused everyone.

He also read Martin's off-centre camera as a sign that Martin was distracted, when Martin had angled it deliberately so that he did not have to look at his own face.

Neither engineer had noticed Femi's discomfort at all, which is the double empathy problem from the other side: they could not read him either.
moreCases.betterRead:
Crompton and colleagues found that chains of autistic people passed on information about as accurately as chains of non-autistic people, while mixed chains lost the most detail. Milton's double empathy problem predicts exactly this: misunderstanding arises in the gap between different ways of communicating, not inside one of them. Ines and Martin shared a style, and the call worked beautifully for them. The only person struggling was Femi, reading it with a map drawn for a different kind of conversation. His better reading would have judged the meeting by what it produced, not by how it felt to him. He deleted the apology. At the next call, he stayed quiet during the silences, took the notes, and asked Ines afterwards whether there was anything he could do to make the meetings easier. She said that not filling the silences would be ideal.

Ines and Martin's project finished a month ahead of schedule.

Femi also learned to send a short agenda before each call, which both engineers said they appreciated.

moreCases.title: The boy who would not look at the teacher
moreCases.scene:
Sami, nine, is autistic, and his class has a supply teacher, Mr Dawson, for two weeks while their usual teacher is on leave. Nobody has passed
  on the information in Sami's support plan. On the first morning, when Mr Dawson is explaining a maths task, he notices that Sami is looking at the
  window rather than at him. He says, "Sami, look at me when I'm talking to you." Sami glances at him and looks away again. Mr Dawson repeats it more
  firmly. Sami's hands start to flap at his sides and he begins to hum.

  Mr Dawson, who has had a difficult year at another school, reads this as defiance. He moves closer, crouches in front of Sami's desk and says,
  "Eyes on me, please." Sami pushes his chair back so hard that it falls over, and runs to the corner of the classroom, where he crouches with his hands
  over his ears.

  The teaching assistant, Mrs Begum, who knows Sami well, goes to him, sits on the floor a little way off and waits. After a few minutes he lets her
  sit beside him. She tells Mr Dawson quietly that Sami listens best when he is not looking at the person speaking, and that he had heard every word of
  the maths explanation.

  That afternoon, Sami's mother, Leila, is called in to discuss his "behaviour".

Leila has been called in about Sami's behaviour before, at another school, and she arrives braced for the same conversation.

Mrs Begum had tried to catch Mr Dawson's eye before he crouched down, but he had not looked at her.

Mr Dawson, for his part, had been told at his last school that he was too soft, and had resolved to be firmer from the first morning at this one.
moreCases.misread:
Mr Dawson read Sami's averted gaze as inattention, and his flapping, humming and retreat as defiance. Each demand for eye contact, made closer and more firmly, raised Sami's distress, and Mr Dawson read the rising distress as worsening behaviour.

The other children read Sami's retreat as Sami being naughty again, which is the reading Mr Dawson had shown them.

Each step in the escalation made sense within Mr Dawson's reading, and each one made Sami's distress worse. A misreading acted on firmly can do more harm than one held lightly.
moreCases.betterRead:
Autistic people often describe eye contact as intense or overwhelming, and many look away in order to listen. Sami's gaze at the window was how he was attending; the flapping and humming were his way of managing a demand he could not meet, and the retreat to the corner was escape from a face pushed close to his. Mr Dawson's reading followed a script that works for many children and failed for this one. The better reading, which the meeting with Leila brought about, began with the support plan. The school made sure every adult who taught Sami had read it, and Mr Dawson apologised to Sami and his mother. He stopped asking any child in the class to look at him while he talked, and found, to his surprise, that several children seemed more settled. Sami finished the maths task the next morning, sitting at the side, looking at the window.

Leila said that the apology mattered to Sami more than anything else, because no adult had ever told him they had got it wrong.

workedReading.title: Meeting a partner's autistic brother
workedReading.scene:
Matt, thirty-three, is spending Christmas with his girlfriend Leah's family for the first time. Her brother, Jonah, twenty-nine, is autistic, and lives with their parents. Leah has told Matt that Jonah is funny, kind and obsessed with trains, that he finds new people tiring, and that previous boyfriends have either ignored him or talked to him as if he were a child. Matt wants to get it right, and he is nervous about getting it wrong. On the drive up, he asks Leah to tell him what helps and what does not, rather than guessing from anything he has read. She tells him three things: Jonah does not like being touched by people he does not know, he does not do much eye contact, and he will talk to you properly if you talk to him about something real. Matt resolves to treat Jonah as a person he is getting to know, not as a condition to be managed.

He also asks Leah what Jonah enjoys doing at Christmas, so that he can join in rather than create something new. She says Jonah likes to do the washing up alone after lunch, and that offering to help would be kind but that he will probably say no.

He also reminds himself that Jonah is an adult, and that the family's habits around him are theirs to explain, not his to correct.

steps.label: Greet without demands
steps.text:
When they arrive, Jonah is in the hallway. Matt smiles, says "Hi, Jonah, I'm Matt, good to meet you," and does not offer his hand or move closer. Jonah says "Hello" to a point somewhere past Matt's shoulder and goes back into the living room. Matt does not read this as rudeness. Leah had told him that Jonah would need time, and a greeting that asks nothing is easier to return later.

Later, when Jonah walks past him in the kitchen, he says "Hi" again, this time on his own terms, and Matt says "Hi" back without making anything of it.

Later in the afternoon, Jonah sits in the same room as Matt for an hour while everyone watches a film. Leah says afterwards that this was a good sign.

steps.label: Let the gaze go
steps.text:
Over lunch, Matt notices that Jonah looks mostly at his plate or the table, even when he is speaking. Matt's habit is to look at people while they talk, and he has to resist the urge to catch Jonah's eye. Part I described how autistic adults often look away in order to concentrate. He lets his own gaze drift to the table too when Jonah speaks, so that Jonah does not feel watched.

He also notices that Jonah listens to everything that is said at the table, and contributes a precise correction to Leah's father's account of a family holiday, which makes everyone laugh, including Jonah.

When Jonah makes a dry joke about the turkey, nobody is quite sure it is a joke until he smiles slightly, and Matt laughs a beat late. Jonah seems pleased.

steps.label: Talk about something real
steps.text:
After lunch, Matt asks Jonah, plainly, which railway line he thinks is the most interesting in the country. Jonah looks up briefly, then launches into a detailed account of a line in Scotland, its engineering and its history. His voice is level and fast. Matt listens, asks two genuine questions and admits he did not know trains could do that. Jonah keeps talking for twenty minutes.

He resists the urge to change the subject when the account becomes very technical. Following someone into the depth of their interest is one of the clearest ways to show respect.

He also notices that Jonah's level voice carries a great deal of enthusiasm once you know what to listen for: speed, detail and the length of the answer.

steps.label: Sit side by side
steps.text:
Later, Jonah is sitting on the sofa looking at a book of railway maps. Matt sits at the other end of the sofa, not too close, and asks whether he can see. Jonah turns the book so that they can both look at it. Side by side, facing the same map, the conversation is easier for both of them than it was face to face across the table, as Part III described for many kinds of difficult talk.

They sit like that for half an hour, mostly in silence, turning the pages. Matt finds it surprisingly restful.

When Jonah points out a branch line that closed in the 1960s, Matt asks why, and gets a ten-minute answer that he genuinely enjoys.

steps.label: Say it plainly
steps.text:
In the evening the family plays a board game, and the jokes come thick and fast. Jonah goes quiet. When Matt makes a sarcastic joke about the rules, Jonah takes it literally and corrects him. Matt laughs and says, "Sorry, I was joking, you're right about the rule." He notices that saying plainly what he means is not a concession; it is a clearer way to talk, and the rest of the family seems to find it easier too.

He also notices that Leah's father, who has known Jonah all his life, still makes sarcastic jokes that Jonah takes literally, and that Leah quietly translates them.

He also avoids teasing Jonah about the correction, which a previous boyfriend, Leah tells him later, had done.

steps.label: Notice your own reading
steps.text:
When Jonah leaves the game halfway through and goes to his room without saying anything, Matt's first reading is that he has done something wrong. He catches the reading and asks Leah instead. She says Jonah has had enough of people for the day, which is normal, and that it is nothing to do with Matt. The double empathy problem, Matt realises, includes his own tendency to take Jonah's behaviour personally.

He also notices that, had he not asked, he would have spent the evening wondering what he had done, and might have been cooler with Jonah the next day.

He decides that the most respectful response is to carry on as normal when Jonah leaves, without comment, and to say goodnight if Jonah comes down again.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
On Boxing Day, Jonah comes down for breakfast and, without preamble, hands Matt a printout of a timetable for a heritage railway near Matt's flat, with two trains circled. Leah tells Matt later that it is the warmest thing she has seen her brother do for a new person. Matt reflects that he did very little: he asked, he waited, he listened, he talked about something real and he did not ask Jonah to look at him.

In February, Matt takes Jonah on the heritage railway. They speak perhaps twenty sentences in four hours, and both of them say afterwards that it was a very good day.

Leah's mother tells Matt that Jonah had asked whether he would be coming next Christmas too.

moreFailures.title: Making the diagnosis the explanation for everything
moreFailures.body:
When someone tells you they are autistic or have ADHD, it can be tempting to attribute everything about them to it. A sharp comment becomes their autism; a forgotten deadline becomes their ADHD; a bad mood becomes a symptom. But neurodivergent people are also people who get tired, annoyed, bored, ill, sad and distracted for all the ordinary reasons, and who have personalities, opinions and days off like anyone else. Reading every behaviour through the diagnosis turns them back into a category, which is exactly what this chapter warns against, and it can excuse real problems that need ordinary attention, or dismiss real feelings as traits. A disclosure tells you something useful about how a person may communicate. It does not tell you why they did a particular thing on a particular day. When you are unsure, ask them, as you would anyone else.

A good check is to ask whether you would read the same behaviour the same way in someone who had not told you anything.

And remember that a person can be autistic and also simply wrong, or simply right, about the thing they are saying.

moreFailures.title: Accommodating by leaving people out
moreFailures.body:
Sometimes, wanting to be considerate, people decide on a neurodivergent colleague's behalf what they can and cannot cope with: not inviting them to the team social because it will be loud, not giving them the client presentation because it involves people, not putting them forward for the promotion because the role involves meetings. It feels like kindness. It is a decision taken without them, and it closes doors they may have wanted open. Many autistic and ADHD people want to take part in exactly these things, with some adjustment, and some do not, and the only way to know is to ask. Offer the invitation and the options: "We're going to the pub on Friday, it'll be busy. Do you want to come, or would you prefer we do something quieter for your leaving do later?" Then respect the answer, whatever it is.

It also helps to remember that "would you like to?" is a much better question than "would you cope?"

If you are planning an event, ask the person what would make it easier for them, and make that change for everyone if you can.

moreFailures.title: Praising someone for not seeming autistic
moreFailures.body:
"You'd never know you were autistic" and "You don't seem like you have ADHD" are usually meant as compliments. To many neurodivergent people, they land very differently. They suggest that the person's natural way of being is something to hide, and that hiding it well is an achievement. They reward masking, the effortful suppression of natural behaviour that the next chapter describes, and which many autistic people say is exhausting and harmful over time. They also imply a picture of what autism or ADHD looks like, usually a narrow one, and tell the person they do not fit it. If you want to say something kind, say it about the person: their work, their humour, their help. If they tell you about their neurodivergence, a simple "Thanks for telling me, is there anything that would help?" is far better than a verdict on how well they pass.

If you notice yourself thinking it, ask what you were expecting autism or ADHD to look like, and where that picture came from.

moreFailures.title: Hearing directness as hostility
moreFailures.body:
Many autistic people, and some people with ADHD, say exactly what they mean without the softening that many others add automatically: "That approach will not work," "This is wrong," "I don't want to do that." To a listener used to cushioned speech, such statements can sound blunt, rude or aggressive, and the listener may react as if they had been attacked. Usually they have not. The speaker is giving information plainly, assuming that the listener wants it, and is often puzzled by the reaction. As the double empathy problem suggests, the misreading lies in the gap between styles. Before taking offence, listen to the content: is it true, useful, relevant? If you need the person to soften feedback in a particular setting, such as with a client, say so plainly and explain why, rather than expecting them to guess. And consider how much time cushioned speech wastes for everyone.

Many teams find that once they get used to a colleague's directness, they prefer it, because they always know where they stand.

If you need softening for a client, model the words you would like used, rather than describing the tone.

questions.q: How can I tell whether someone is autistic or has ADHD?
questions.a:
You usually cannot, and you do not need to. Diagnosis is a careful process carried out by trained clinicians, and the behaviours in this chapter, such as averted gaze, fidgeting or a level voice, are common in many people for many reasons. Deciding that someone is autistic or has ADHD on the strength of their manner turns a person into a label and is often wrong. What you can do is respond to the person in front of you: notice if your usual reading of their behaviour might not fit, ask rather than infer, state your meaning plainly and offer different ways of taking part. If someone tells you they are neurodivergent, thank them and ask what helps. If you wonder about yourself, the final question in this chapter covers that.

And if someone does not tell you, that is their choice. They owe nobody an explanation of how their mind works.

questions.q: Should I avoid eye contact with an autistic person?
questions.a:
Follow their lead rather than a rule. Many autistic people find sustained eye contact uncomfortable or distracting, so do not demand it, do not comment on it and do not read its absence as disinterest. But you do not need to avoid looking at them altogether; ordinary, brief glances are usually fine, and some autistic people are comfortable with eye contact. A useful habit is to let your gaze rest on something shared, such as a document, a screen or the view, as Matt did with the railway maps, so that neither of you has to manage a face-to-face stare. Talking side by side or while walking can make conversation easier for many people, autistic or not. If you are unsure, it is fine to ask what is comfortable.

If you are speaking to an autistic child, the same applies even more strongly. Never make eye contact a condition of being listened to.

And never comment on someone's eye contact, approvingly or otherwise, unless they raise it.

questions.q: What if I genuinely find a colleague's manner difficult?
questions.a:
Start by separating the manner from the substance. The Words Without the Body drill in this chapter is useful here: write down what the colleague actually said and did, and read it as if it came from a stranger. Sasson and colleagues found that observers judged autistic adults less favourably from short video clips but not from transcripts of the same words. Your difficulty may be with the style rather than the person. Then remember that the misunderstanding runs both ways; your manner may be just as hard for them to read. If something is causing a real problem, talk about it plainly and specifically: "When you say my plan won't work in front of the client, it makes it harder for me. Could you tell me first?" Agree ways of working, rather than trying to change who someone is.

It also helps to ask how they prefer to receive feedback, which tells you something useful and shows respect.

If you manage the colleague, ask yourself whether you are judging their work or their style, and keep the two apart in any review.

questions.q: How can I tell what an autistic person is feeling?
questions.a:
Often, by asking, and by learning that particular person's ways of showing things over time. Brewer, Bird and colleagues found that autistic people's facial expressions were hard for everyone to read, autistic observers included, because each person's face had its own style. So general rules about autistic expressions will not help much. What helps is the same principle this book applies to everyone: learn the person's baseline. Notice what they do when they are content, stressed, absorbed or tired. Many autistic people will tell you directly how they feel if you ask a clear question, such as "Are you OK to keep going, or would you like a break?" They may also show feelings through actions rather than faces, as Rosie did with the animals and Jonah did with the timetable.

It is worth remembering that the same is true of everyone. Nobody's face is a reliable window, which is why asking is always useful.

Over time, many people find they can read an autistic friend or colleague very well, once they stop expecting the usual signals.

questions.q: Is fidgeting in a meeting rude?
questions.a:
Not in itself. For many people, and especially for some people with ADHD, movement helps them concentrate: Sarver and colleagues found that children with ADHD who moved more while doing demanding memory tasks tended to perform better. Leg-bouncing, doodling, turning a pen or pacing at the back of the room may be signs of someone working hard to listen, as Kieran was. Many autistic people also use repetitive movements to regulate their arousal and focus. Unless the movement genuinely disrupts others, for example by making a loud noise, it is better to let it be. If you chair meetings, you can make it normal by saying that people are welcome to stand, move or fiddle with something if it helps them think.

If a fidget does make noise, such as a clicking pen, offer a quieter alternative rather than asking the person to stop moving.

And if you notice yourself fidgeting more when concentrating, that may be your own body helping you.

questions.q: I think I might be neurodivergent myself. What should I do?
questions.a:
You do not need to decide alone, and you do not need to rely on online quizzes or descriptions of other people. If you think you may be autistic or have ADHD, and it would help you to know, talk to your GP or doctor about an assessment; waiting times can be long, but a doctor can explain the options. In the meantime, many people find it useful to read accounts by neurodivergent people themselves and to connect with communities run by and for them. You do not need a diagnosis to make changes that help you, such as asking for agendas in advance, moving while you think, taking breaks from noisy places or working in writing where you can. Whatever an assessment finds, the aim is to understand yourself better, not to fit a label.

Whatever you find, be gentle with yourself about the years before you knew. Many people describe a mix of relief and grief.

If an assessment is not possible, or you decide against one, the adjustments that help are still worth making.

watch.title: Love on the Spectrum: Official Trailer
watch.notice: Autistic adults on first dates, speaking for themselves. Notice the range: some look away while listening, some speak in level tones about things they love, some say exactly what they think. Then notice how much warmth there is, once you stop reading it through the usual map.

watch.title: The world needs all kinds of minds
watch.notice: An autistic scientist speaking to a large audience. Notice her direct, unadorned delivery and her gaze, and how quickly the content takes over from the manner if you let it.

reviewPrompt: This week, judge one person by what they say and do rather than their manner, and replace one hint with a plain statement.
